evidence: "Aristophanes professed to open another vein of discourse; he had a mind to praise Love"
"have never, as I think, at all understood the power of Love"
"let me treat of the nature of man and what has happened to it"
"the word Androgynous is only preserved as a term of reproach"
"the primeval man was round"
"two sets of privy members, and the remainder to correspond"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: say plainly that Aristophanes set out to praise Love in a different way; untangle 'have never, as I think, at all understood'; explain that 'androgynous' means man-woman and survives only as an insult; make clear 'the primeval man' means every original human being of all three kinds; plain words for the doubled genitals and 'everything else to match'.

evidence: "like tumblers going over and over with their legs in the air"
"Terrible was their might and strength, and the thoughts of their hearts were great"
"Of them is told the tale of Otys and Ephialtes who, as Homer says, dared to scale heaven"
"the gods could not suffer their insolence to be unrestrained"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: make 'tumblers' acrobats turning cartwheels (today it suggests drinking glasses); un-invert 'Terrible was their might' and 'Of them is told the tale' and say plainly their pride/ambition was huge; identify Otys and Ephialtes as the giant brothers who tried to storm heaven; replace 'could not suffer their insolence to be unrestrained' with a plain 'could not let their arrogance go unchecked'.

evidence: "like a sorb-apple which is halved for pickling"
"he bade Apollo give the face and the half of the neck a turn, in order that the man might contemplate the section of himself"
"Apollo was also bidden to heal their wounds and compose their forms"
"like the purses which draw in, and he made one mouth at the center"
"much as a shoemaker might smooth leather upon a last"
"being the sections of entire men or women, and clung to that"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: keep every simile but make each intelligible in a few words (sorb-apple = a small fruit halved for pickling; a drawstring purse; a shoemaker's last = foot-shaped form); say Apollo turned each face toward its cut side so the person could see it; 'opening' for 'mouth'; 'reshape their bodies' for 'compose their forms'; untangle 'being the sections of entire men or women'.

evidence: "he turned the parts of generation round to the front"
"they sowed the seed no longer as hitherto like grasshoppers in the ground"
"is but the indenture of a man"
"the female companions are of this sort"
"But they who are a section of the male follow the male"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: replace 'indenture' (today a contract) with the image Jowett means, one half of a split token looking for its match; plain words for genitals and reproduction; make the insect image clear (creatures thought to breed in the earth); make clear 'the female companions' are women who love women; 'those who' for 'they who'.

evidence: "they do not act thus from any want of shame"
"they are lovers of youth, and are not naturally inclined to marry or beget children"
"whether he be a lover of youth or a lover of another sort"
"as I may say, even for a moment"
"something else which the soul of either evidently desires and cannot tell, and of which she has only a dark and doubtful presentiment"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: say plainly that as grown men they take younger male partners rather than marry (what 'lovers of youth' means; today it could read as 'fond of youthfulness'); 'lack of shame'; 'have children'; end with a clear sentence that each soul longs for something it cannot put into words and only dimly senses.

evidence: "Suppose Hephaestus, with his instruments, to come to the pair who are lying side by side"
"There is not a man of them who, when he heard the proposal, would deny or would not acknowledge that"
"as the Arcadians were dispersed into villages by the Lacedaemonians"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'Suppose Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, came with his tools...'; turn the double negative into a plain 'every one of them would agree that'; identify the Lacedaemonians as the Spartans who broke the Arcadians' city up into villages.

evidence: "go about in basso-relievo, like the profile figures with only half a nose which are sculptured on monuments, and that we shall be like tallies"
"Wherefore let us exhort all men to piety"
"of which Love is to us the lord and minister"
"he is the enemy of the gods who opposes him"
"the best in the next degree and under present circumstances"
"the attainment of a congenial love"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: explain the images in a few words (flat carved figures in profile on monuments; tallies = split tokens that only match their other half); 'So let us urge everyone to reverence'; 'whoever opposes Love is the gods' enemy'; 'the next best thing, as things are now'; make 'congenial love' a partner whose nature truly matches ours, not merely a pleasant one.

evidence: "Wherefore, if we would praise him who has given to us this benefit"
"This, Eryximachus, is my discourse of love"
"leave unassailed by the shafts of your ridicule"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'So if we want to praise the one who has done us this good...'; 'my speech about love'; a plainer 'not to make it a target for your jokes'; keep the 'each, or rather either' joke about the two speakers left.

paragraphs.note: Clear conversational line; the formal 'did I not know' is readable by eye and ear.

evidence: "you would indeed be in a great strait"
paragraphs.fix: Light: replace 'in a great strait' (now suggests a sea channel) with a plain 'in real difficulty' or similar; use the same wording wherever Socrates' 'strait' recurs (6.7, 6.8, 6.9).

paragraphs.note: Long but followable in one hearing; optional polish only ('compositions ... exhibited' = plays staged; 'magnanimity' here = self-assurance).

evidence: "'Nay,' replied Socrates"
"that or any other want of refinement"
"if you happened to meet with any whom you thought wise"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'No' for 'Nay'; 'lack of taste' for 'want of refinement'; 'met people you thought wise'; keep Socrates' trap question intact.

evidence: "I must not forget the encomium on Love which I ought to receive from him and from every one"
paragraphs.fix: Light: replace or gloss 'encomium' (its first use; the proposal in 1.46 said 'a speech in honor of Love') as 'speech in praise of Love'; leave the rest as is.

paragraphs.note: Clear. Mechanical only: the closing quote after 'then speak:—' leaves Agathon's speech (6.0–6.6) unquoted.

evidence: "he is the most blessed, because he is the fairest and best"
"fleeing out of the way of age, who is swift enough — swifter truly than most of us like. Love hates him and will not come near him"
"I cannot agree that he is older than Iapetus and Kronos"
"if the tradition of them be true, were done of Necessity"
"there would have been no chaining or mutilation of the gods"
"as Homer says of Ate, that she is a goddess and tender"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'most beautiful' for 'fairest' (today it reads as 'most just'); name Age as the swift one Love hates so 'him' is unambiguous; add a few words identifying Iapetus and Kronos as ancient Titans, the chaining and mutilation as the old myths of divine violence told by Hesiod and Parmenides, and Ate as the goddess of ruin; 'if the stories are true, were the work of Necessity'.

paragraphs.note: Homer's verse on Ate, kept as quotation; clear once 6.0 says who Ate is.

evidence: "herein is an excellent proof of her tenderness"
"Let us adduce a similar proof"
"Of a truth he is the tenderest as well as the youngest, and also he is of flexile form; for if he were hard and without flexure"
"ungrace and love are always at war"
"whether of body or soul or aught else"
"The fairness of his complexion is revealed by his habitation among the flowers"
paragraphs.fix: Recast in present-day wording (this proves; let me offer; truly; supple; gracelessness; anything else) and make 'the fairness of his complexion' the beauty of his colouring, not pale skin; keep the soft/hard and flower images in order.

evidence: "for he suffers not by force if he suffers — force comes not near him, neither when he acts does he act by force"
"exceedingly temperate; for Temperance is the acknowledged ruler of the pleasures and desires"
"masters him, as the tale runs"
"I magnify my art"
"the source of poesy in others"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: state plainly that nothing is done to Love by force and he does nothing by force; 'self-controlled/self-control' for temperate/Temperance; name Ares as the God of War held captive by his love for Aphrodite; 'praise my own art'; 'poetry' for 'poesy'.

evidence: "he only of them whom love inspires has the light of fame? He whom Love touches not walks in darkness"
"for with deformity Love has no concern"
"and from the Love of the beautiful, has sprung every good in heaven and earth"
"he is the fairest and best in himself"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'only the artist Love inspires wins fame; the one Love never touches stays in obscurity'; 'ugliness' for 'deformity' (today a physical malformation); un-invert 'has sprung every good'; 'most beautiful' for 'fairest'; keep the list of the gods' arts and the lead-in to the verse.

paragraphs.note: Verse quotation; poetic register is appropriate and clear.
Agathon's deliberately ornate, Gorgias-style litany; clear by eye and ear and part of Plato's characterisation. Optional only: 'makes them to meet together' -> 'brings them together'.

evidence: "When Agathon had done speaking"
"that I should be in a strait"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'had finished speaking'; replace 'in a strait' with the same plain phrase chosen for 5.9.

evidence: "that you will be in a strait"
paragraphs.fix: Light: same replacement for 'in a strait' as in 5.9 and 6.7; keep the rest.

evidence: "must not I or anyone be in a strait who has to speak after he has heard such a rich and varied discourse"
"shaking at me the Gorginian or Gorgonian head of the great master of rhetoric"
"that, this being presupposed, out of the true the speaker was to choose the best and set them forth in the best manner"
"every species of greatness and glory"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: a plain question ('wouldn't anyone be at a loss...'); a few words so the pun works (Agathon's style echoes the orator Gorgias, and Socrates fears a Gorgon's head that turns listeners to stone); lay out his old view of praise in order: tell the truth, choose the finest truths, arrange them well; 'every kind of'.

evidence: "making him appear the fairest and best of all to those who know him not"
"for you cannot impose upon those who know him"
"And a noble and solemn hymn of praise have you rehearsed"
"Farewell then to such a strain"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'most beautiful'; 'to people who do not know him'; 'you cannot fool' for 'impose upon'; 'what a noble, solemn hymn you have delivered' ('rehearsed' now means practised); 'goodbye to that style of praise'; keep the Euripides lips/mind line.

paragraphs.note: Clear; 'bid him speak' is dated but transparent, and 'premises of my discourse' is readable.

evidence: "I don't want you to say that love is the love of a father or the love of a mother — that would be ridiculous."
"But to answer as you would if I asked, is a father a father of something? To which you would find no difficulty in replying, of a son or daughter"
paragraphs.fix: Recast the last three sentences: make clear the ridiculous question Socrates rules out is Love's parentage (whose child Love is), not love felt for a parent, and replace the two sentence fragments with full sentences that keep the father-of-a-son-or-daughter analogy.

paragraphs.note: Clear in the context of the father/brother examples.

evidence: "Keep in mind what this is"
"whether Love desires that of which love is"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'keep in mind what love is love of', then ask plainly whether Love desires the very thing it is love of.

evidence: "I would have you consider whether necessarily is not rather the word"
"'Nay,' replied Socrates"
paragraphs.fix: Light: restore the quotation marks (or italics) around 'necessarily', lost in modernization so the sentence no longer parses, and set it against Agathon's 'probably'; 'No' for 'Nay'; 'I'd like you to consider'; keep the desire-implies-lack inference.

paragraphs.note: Clear: no one wants to be what he already is.

evidence: "if a man being strong desired to be strong, or being swift desired to be swift, or being healthy desired to be healthy"
"the possessors of these qualities, Agathon, must be supposed to have their respective advantages at the time, whether they choose or not"
"want to have the continuance of them"
"whether you choose or no"
paragraphs.fix: Recast in plain syntax: a strong man who says he wants to be strong seems to want what he has, but he has it now whether he likes it or not, so what he wants is to keep it in the future; keep all three examples, the imagined reply and the closing check.

paragraphs.note: Followable conclusion; 'preserved to him' is dated but clear.

evidence: "desires that which he has not already, and which is future and not present, and which he has not, and is not, and of which he is in want"
paragraphs.fix: Recast as a clear list keeping every item in order: what he does not already have, what is future not present, what he is not, what he lacks.

evidence: "and of something too which is wanting to a man"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'wanting to a man' means 'which a person lacks' but now reads as 'wanting to (do)'; say 'something the person lacks'.

evidence: "for that of deformed things there is no love"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'because there is no love of ugly things'; match the repaired wording of Agathon's claim in 6.4, which Socrates is quoting.

evidence: "Love is the love of beauty and not of deformity"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'ugliness' for 'deformity' (today a physical malformation), matching 6.4 and 7.28.

paragraphs.note: 'wants and has not' reads naturally as 'wants and does not have', which is the point; formal but clear.
Terse but clear whichever way 'wants' is read; optional 'does not have'.
Clear; 'does not possess' carries the logic.

evidence: "one small question which I would fain ask"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'one small question I would like to ask'; keep the rest.

evidence: "Then in wanting the beautiful, love wants also the good?"
paragraphs.fix: Light: use 'lacking/lacks' so the step reads 'if Love lacks beauty, it also lacks the good'; as written 'wants' reads as 'desires' and hides the conclusion that Love is not good.

evidence: "Say rather, beloved Agathon"
paragraphs.fix: Light: replace 'Say rather' with a present-day turn meaning 'No — it is the truth you cannot refute'; keep 'beloved Agathon' and 'Socrates is easily refuted'.

evidence: "I would rehearse a tale of love"
"She was my instructress in the art of love"
"that Love was a mighty god, and likewise fair"
"by my own showing, Love was neither fair nor good"
"is love then evil and foul?"
"must that be foul which is not fair?"
"there is a mean between wisdom and ignorance"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'tell you a story' ('rehearse' now means practise); use 'beautiful'/'ugly' for fair/foul so the recap visibly repeats the Agathon argument just finished; 'teacher'; 'by my own argument'; 'something in between' for 'a mean'; keep the plague detail and 'I shall take both parts'.

evidence: "which, as you know, being incapable of giving a reason, is not knowledge (for how can knowledge be devoid of reason? Nor again, ignorance, for neither can ignorance attain the truth)"
"that what is not fair is of necessity foul, or what is not good evil"
"for he is in a mean between them"
"the gods are happy and fair"
"who has no portion in what is either good or fair"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: explain right opinion in plain sentences (being right without being able to give the reason, so neither knowledge nor ignorance); 'beautiful'/'ugly' for fair/foul throughout; 'in between'; 'has no share in'; keep every step of the argument that Socrates too denies Love is a god.

evidence: "he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in a mean between the two"
"For God mingles not with man; but through Love all the intercourse and converse of God with man"
"all other wisdom, such as that of arts and handicrafts, is mean and vulgar"
"who is the son of Metis or Discretion"
"as the manner is on such occasions, came about the doors to beg"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'in between'; 'God does not mix with humans; all communication and conversation between them...' ('intercourse' now reads as sex); 'lowly and workaday' for 'mean and vulgar' (not unkind or crude); gloss Metis as cunning intelligence ('Discretion' now means tact); 'as beggars do at a feast, came to the door to beg'; keep the list of priestly arts and '(daimon)'.

evidence: "Now Plenty who was the worse for nectar"
"conceived Love, who partly because he is naturally a lover of the beautiful, and because Aphrodite is herself beautiful, and also because he was born on her birthday, is her follower and attendant"
"And as his parentage is, so also are his fortunes"
"anything but tender and fair, as the many imagine him"
"on the bare earth exposed he lies under the open heaven"
"he is always plotting against the fair and good"
"terrible as an enchanter, sorcerer, sophist"
"by reason of his father's nature"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: split the long clause giving the three reasons Love follows Aphrodite; 'schemes to win the beautiful and the good' (today 'plotting against' means trying to harm them); 'formidable' for 'terrible'; a few words on 'sophist' (clever professional arguer); 'beautiful' for 'fair'; un-invert the sleeping-rough image; 'drunk on nectar'; keep every trait in order.

evidence: "he is in a mean between ignorance and knowledge"
"For herein is the evil of ignorance"
"And of this too his birth is the cause"
"has arisen out of a confusion of love and the beloved"
"but the principle of love is of another nature"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'in between'; 'this is what is bad about ignorance'; 'his birth explains this too'; make explicit that Socrates confused the lover, who lacks and longs, with the beloved, who is beautiful and blessed; keep the philosopher = lover of wisdom gloss.

evidence: "O thou stranger woman, thou sayest well"
"Of the beautiful in what, Socrates and Diotima?"
"let me put the word good in the place of the beautiful"
"And what does he gain who possesses the good?"
paragraphs.fix: Light: a present-day address to Diotima as a visitor from abroad ('Well said...'; 'stranger' now means someone unknown); make the imagined question plain (what is it about beautiful things that love wants?); restore the marking of 'good' as a word (quotation marks lost in modernization); 'what does someone who has the good gain?'.

evidence: "What say you?"
"Whereas you say that all men are always loving the same things."
"All creation or passage of non-being into being is poetry or making, and the processes of all art are creative; and the masters of arts are all poets or makers."
"they who possess poetry in this sense of the word are called poets"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: add a few words that the Greek word for poetry literally means 'making', so every craftsman is strictly a 'poet' though the name is kept for verse-makers, which is the model for how 'love' is used; turn the 'Whereas' fragment into a full sentence; 'What do you say?'; 'those who'.

evidence: "they who are drawn toward him by any other path, whether the path of money-making or gymnastics or philosophy"
"the name of the whole is appropriated to those whose affection takes one form only"
"unless the half or the whole be also a good"
"for they love not what is their own, unless perchance there be some one who calls what belongs to him the good, and what belongs to another the evil"
"Certainly, I should say, that there is nothing."
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'only those whose love takes one particular form get the general name'; 'athletics' for 'gymnastics'; make the step plain that people do not love what is theirs just because it is theirs, unless someone counts his own as good and another's as bad; keep the rebuttal of the 'other half', the hands-and-feet example and the build-up to 'everlasting possession of the good'.

evidence: "Then if this be the nature of love"
"Nay, Diotima"
"neither should I have come to learn from you"
"all men are bringing to the birth in their bodies and in their souls"
"procreation which must be in beauty and not in deformity"
"and in the inharmonious they can never be. But the deformed is always inharmonious with the divine"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'all human beings are pregnant, in body and in soul'; 'ugliness'/'the ugly' for deformity/the deformed; 'these cannot happen in what is out of harmony with the divine'; 'reproduction' for 'generation'; 'No, Diotima'; keep 'birth in beauty' as Diotima's riddle and Socrates' 'the oracle needs explaining'.

evidence: "Beauty, then, is the destiny or goddess of parturition who presides at birth"
"the conceiving power is propitious, and diffusive, and benign"
"when the hour of conception arrives, and the teeming nature is full"
"the alleviation of the pain of travail"
"The love of generation and of birth in beauty."
"wherefore love is of immortality"
paragraphs.fix: Recast in plain childbirth language: Beauty is the Fate and birth-goddess presiding over birth; near beauty the pregnant creature relaxes, opens and gives birth, near ugliness it shrinks and holds back; 'labour pains' for 'travail'; 'reproduction' for 'generation' (today an age group); 'so love is also of immortality'.

evidence: "See you not how all animals"
"whereto is added the care of offspring"
"even to the uttermost"
"if you believe that love is of the immortal, as we have several times acknowledged"
"this is only to be attained by generation, because generation always leaves behind a new existence in the place of the old"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'Don't you see...'; 'then comes care for their young'; 'to the death'; turn 'Marvel not ... if you believe' into a clear conditional (if you really believe love is of the immortal, do not be surprised); 'reproduction' for 'generation'.

evidence: "Nay, even in the life of the same individual there is succession and not absolute unity"
"a perpetual process of loss and reparation"
"not only do the sciences in general spring up and decay"
"but the departure of knowledge, which is ever being forgotten, and is renewed and preserved by recollection, and appears to be the same although in reality new"
"partakes of immortality; but the immortal in another way"
paragraphs.fix: Recast into shorter sentences: even one person's body, soul and knowledge are constantly lost and replaced; we need 'recollection' because knowledge leaves us and is replaced by new, similar knowledge; mortals share in immortality by such replacement, unlike the divine, which stays the same; 'loss and renewal'; 'branches of knowledge' for 'sciences'.

evidence: "Marvel not then at the love which all men have of their offspring"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'So do not be surprised that everyone loves their children', matching the wording chosen for 'Marvel not' in 7.55; keep 'for the sake of immortality'.

evidence: "Is this really true, O thou wise Diotima?"
"with all the authority of an accomplished sophist"
"ready to run all risks greater far than they would have run for their children"
"or your own Codrus in order to preserve the kingdom for his sons"
paragraphs.fix: Light: drop 'O thou'; a few words on 'sophist' (a professional teacher of wisdom, said with irony); 'far greater risks'; identify Codrus as the early king of Athens who died to save it; 'Indeed' for the second 'Nay'; Alcestis and Achilles need nothing, being familiar from Phaedrus's speech.

evidence: "betake themselves to women and beget children"
"the greatest and fairest sort of wisdom by far"
"which is called temperance and justice"
"desires to beget and generate"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'turn to women and have children'; 'most beautiful' for 'fairest'; 'moderation' or 'self-control' for 'temperance' (today it suggests teetotalism); 'wants to beget offspring'; keep the body/soul pregnancy contrast and the poets and inventors.

evidence: "for in deformity he will beget nothing — and naturally embraces the beautiful rather than the deformed body"
"when he finds a fair and noble and well-nurtured soul"
"to such an one he is full of speech about virtue"
"he brings forth that which he had conceived long before"
"they are married by a far nearer tie"
"such children as Lycurgus left behind him to be the saviors, not only of Lacedaemon, but of Hellas"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'ugliness'/'ugly' for deformity/deformed; 'beautiful' for 'fair'; 'to such a person he talks freely about virtue'; 'gives birth to what he conceived long ago'; 'a far closer bond'; identify Lycurgus as Sparta's lawgiver whose 'children' are his laws, and Lacedaemon and Hellas as Sparta and Greece.

evidence: "many others there are in many other places, both among Hellenes and barbarians"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'Greeks and non-Greeks' ('barbarians' here means foreigners, not savages); un-invert 'many others there are'; keep Solon and the temples point.

evidence: "These are the lesser mysteries of love"
"to the greater and more hidden ones which are the crown of these, and to which, if you pursue them in a right spirit, they will lead, I know not whether you will be able to attain"
"For he who would proceed aright in this matter should begin in youth to visit beautiful forms"
"if he be guided by his instructor aright, to love one such form only — out of that he should create fair thoughts"
"he will abate his violent love of the one, which he will despise and deem a small thing"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: a few words on the lesser and greater mysteries as the first and final stages of a religious initiation; 'bodies' for 'forms' here (a reader will take 'forms' as Plato's Forms); split the 'I know not whether you will be able to attain' sentence; 'rightly' for 'aright'; 'beautiful thoughts'; 'let go of his intense passion for one person, thinking it small'; keep each step of the ascent in order.

evidence: "So that if a virtuous soul have but a little comeliness, he will be content to love and tend him"
"bring to the birth thoughts which may improve the young"
"that personal beauty is a trifle"
"he will go on to the sciences"
"being not like a servant in love with the beauty of one youth or man or institution, himself a slave mean and narrow-minded, but drawing toward and contemplating the vast sea of beauty"
"until on that shore he grows and waxes strong"
"a single science, which is the science of beauty everywhere"
"please to give me your very best attention"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'even if someone with a good soul has little physical beauty' (and fix the soul/him pronoun shift); 'give birth to thoughts'; 'bodily beauty is a small thing'; 'branches of knowledge' and 'knowledge of beauty' for sciences/science; split the petty-slave versus vast-sea contrast into clear sentences; 'grows strong'; 'please give me'.

evidence: "the final cause of all our former toils"
"not fair in one point of view and foul in another"
"as if fair to some and foul to others, or in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the bodily frame"
"He who from these ascending under the influence of true love begins to perceive that beauty, is not far from the end."
paragraphs.fix: Recast keeping the whole cumulative list and its rhythm: 'beautiful'/'ugly' for fair/foul; repeat the negative so each item clearly says what this beauty is not (not a face, not a speech, not in any other thing); 'the goal of all our earlier efforts' for 'final cause'; un-invert the last sentence.

evidence: "and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions"
"said the stranger of Mantineia"
"you would see not to be after the measure of gold, and garments, and fair boys and youths"
"you and many a one would be content to live seeing them only and conversing with them without meat or drink"
"thither looking, and holding converse with the true beauty simple and divine?"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: the ladder as beautiful bodies, beautiful practices, beautiful notions, then beauty itself (keep every step); 'the woman from Mantinea' ('stranger' now means someone unknown); 'not to be measured against gold and clothes'; 'food' for 'meat'; turn the final 'thither looking' question into plain modern syntax.

evidence: "he will be enabled to bring forth, not images of beauty, but realities"
"and bringing forth and nourishing true virtue to become the friend of God and be immortal, if mortal man may"
paragraphs.fix: Recast in two clear sentences: only there can he give birth to realities, not images, because he is in touch with reality; and by bringing forth and nurturing true virtue he can become the friend of God and immortal, if any human can; keep the closing question.

evidence: "I say that every man ought to honor him as I myself honor him, and walk in his ways, and exhort others to do the same, and praise the power and spirit of love according to the measure of my ability, now and ever"
paragraphs.fix: Light: separate what every man ought to do (honor Love) from what Socrates himself does (honors Love, walks in his ways, urges others to do the same, praises Love as well as he can, now and always), so 'my ability' no longer attaches to 'every man'.

evidence: "may call an encomium of love"
paragraphs.fix: Light: render or gloss 'encomium' as 'a speech in praise of love', consistent with 5.16; keep Socrates' ironic 'or anything else which you please'.

evidence: "When Socrates had done speaking"
"in answer to the allusion which Socrates had made to his own speech"
"as of revellers"
"his head flowing with ribands"
"this fairest and wisest of men, as I may be allowed to call him"
"shall we have the understanding of which I spoke?"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'had finished speaking'; make clear the allusion was to Aristophanes' own speech (the 'other half'); 'like a party of revellers'; 'ribbons'; 'handsomest' for 'fairest'; 'will you accept the terms I mentioned?' (being received drunk); keep the garland, the crowning plan and the drunken bluster.

paragraphs.note: Plain line. Mechanical only: no opening quote mark although Alcibiades' speech continues from 8.0.

evidence: "he took the ribands from his own head"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'ribbons', matching 8.0 and 8.5; the rest (including 'make a third on the same couch') reads clearly and should stay.

evidence: "but by the fairest of the company?"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'the best-looking person here' (Agathon), since 'fairest' can read as 'most just'; optional 'unexpected' for 'unsuspected'; keep the rest.

evidence: "I have never been allowed to speak to any other fair one"
"not only abuses me but can hardly keep his hands off me"
"Please to see to this"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'insults me and can barely keep from hitting me' (today 'abuses me' and 'can hardly keep his hands off me' suggest abuse or sexual groping); 'anyone else good-looking'; 'Please see to this'; keep Socrates' mock plea for protection.

evidence: "for the present I will defer your chastisement"
"give me back some of the ribands"
"I would not have him complain of me"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'for now I'll put off punishing you'; 'ribbons'; 'I don't want him complaining that...'; keep 'universal despot' and 'conqueror of all mankind'.

paragraphs.note: Clear narrative and dialogue; 'bade' is dated but transparent.
Mock-heroic greeting is deliberate; 'sire' is clear from 'son of'.
Pope's line from Homer kept as quotation; the doctor joke is clear from 'shall prescribe' in 8.12.
Clear; 'have well drunken' keeps Jowett's spoken/drunken jingle and is transparent.

evidence: "he will hardly keep his hands off me"
paragraphs.fix: Light: make plain that Socrates would get violent (e.g. 'can hardly keep from hitting me'), matching 8.4; today the phrase reads as sexual attraction.

paragraphs.note: 'For shame' is dated but clear as a rebuke.
Clear; 'when you are of the company' = when you are present.

evidence: "if you like praise Socrates"
paragraphs.fix: Light: punctuate or reorder so it reads 'then praise Socrates, if you like'; without the comma it parses as 'if you like praise'.

paragraphs.note: 'What are you about?' is dated but explained by the next two questions.

evidence: "you must not wonder if I speak any how as things come into my mind"
"the fluent and orderly enumeration of all your singularities"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'don't be surprised if I jump around as things come to me' ('wonder if' now means 'ask whether'); 'listing all your oddities smoothly and in order' ('singularities' is now a technical term).

evidence: "I shall praise Socrates in a figure"
"the busts of Silenus, which are set up in the statuaries' shops"
"Aye, and there is a resemblance in other points too"
"you are a bully"
"for the melodies of Olympus are derived from Marsyas who taught them"
"they alone possess the soul and reveal the wants of those who have need of gods and mysteries"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'by means of an image'; a few words on the Silenus figures (hollow statuettes of the pot-bellied old satyr, sold in sculptors' shops, that open to show gods inside); 'insolent' or 'outrageous' for 'bully' (today someone who intimidates the weak); 'Olympus, Marsyas's pupil' (not the mountain); say plainly that these tunes seize listeners and reveal who needs the gods and their rites; 'Yes' for 'Aye'.

evidence: "more than that of any Corybantian reveller"
"I would have sworn as well as spoken to the influence"
"has often brought me to such a pass"
"fly as from the voice of the siren"
paragraphs.fix: Light: a few words for the Corybantian revellers (worshippers dancing in religious frenzy); 'I would swear to the effect'; 'driven me to the point'; 'flee as from the Sirens' song'; the rest (Pericles, the confession) reads well and should stay.

paragraphs.note: Clear, direct confession; 'fly from him' is made plain by 'run away'.

evidence: "but I will reveal him to you, having begun, I must go on"
"See you how fond he is of the fair?"
"what temperance there is residing within!"
"Know you that beauty and wealth and honor"
"he regards not at all the persons who are gifted with them"
"mocking and flouting at them"
paragraphs.fix: Light: restore a full stop before 'having begun' (the modern comma creates a run-on); 'Do you see how he is drawn to beautiful young men?'; 'self-control' for 'temperance' (at a drinking party it reads as abstinence); 'Believe me'; 'he does not care at all about'; 'mocking and scorning'.

evidence: "In the prosecution of this design"
"do you, Socrates, expose the falsehood"
"I challenged him to the palaestra, and he wrestled and closed with me"
"as I had failed hitherto"
"just as if he were a fair youth, and I a designing lover"
"I had not the face to detain him"
"still in pursuance of my design"
"he had much better remain"
paragraphs.fix: Recast in plain narrative: 'to carry out this plan'; 'you, Socrates, must expose'; 'the wrestling school' and 'grappled with me'; 'so far'; make the role reversal explicit (as if he were the handsome youth and I the older lover pursuing him); 'dinner' for 'sup'; 'I didn't have the nerve to keep him'; 'still following my plan'; 'he had much better stay'.

evidence: "the same on which he had supped"
"no one but ourselves sleeping in the apartment"
"whether with boys, or without them"
"bitten by a more than viper's tooth"
"more violent in ingenuous youth"
"other profane and unmannered persons"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: 'room' for 'apartment'; spell out the proverb (wine, with or without children, both said to tell the truth); 'more painful to a gifted young mind' ('ingenuous' now means naive); 'the uninitiated' for 'profane', as at the mysteries; 'dined'; keep the snakebite image and the list of those present.

evidence: "Do you know what I am meditating?"
"of all the lovers whom I have ever had"
"you will have greatly the advantage of me"
"like Diomede, gold in exchange for brass"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'what I've been thinking of doing' ('meditating' now means a calming practice); 'admirers' for 'lovers' (men who courted him, not sexual partners); 'you'll get much the better of the bargain'; a few words on Diomedes' famous trade of bronze armour for gold in Homer; keep the offer and Socrates' ironic reply complete.

evidence: "The mind begins to grow critical when the bodily eye fails"
"and do you consider what you think best for you and me"
"he was so superior to my solicitations"
"hear, O judges; for judges you shall be of the haughty virtue of Socrates — nothing more happened"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: make the eyesight contrast explicit (the mind's eye sharpens as the body's eyes dim, and you are far from old); 'you decide what is best'; 'so unmoved by my advances'; break the long interrupted sentence so 'nothing more happened' lands clearly after the appeal to the judges; keep 'wonderful monster' (extraordinary being) and the father/brother ending.

evidence: "I could not help wondering at his natural temperance"
"if Ajax could not be wounded by steel, much less he by money"
"the expedition to Potidaea; there we messed together"
"wonderful to relate!"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'marvelling at his self-control' ('wondering at' and 'temperance' now mislead); unpack the Ajax comparison (money could wound him even less than weapons could wound Ajax); 'the campaign at Potidaea'; 'we shared the army's mess'; 'amazingly'; keep the hunger, drinking and cold details.

paragraphs.note: Vivid and clear; 'well shod' and 'looked daggers' are transparent.
Plain; the sentence runs through the Homer line (8.34) into 8.35.
Homeric quotation (said of Odysseus); meaning clear in context.

evidence: "this, again, Socrates will not impeach or deny"
"he rescued me and my arms"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'dispute or deny' ('impeach' now means charging an official); 'me and my weapons'; otherwise keep the paragraph as is.

evidence: "and there you might see him, Aristophanes, as you describe him"
"He and Laches were retreating"
"where he served among the heavy-armed"
"making very intelligible to anybody, even from a distance"
"Many are the marvels which I might narrate"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'as you portray him in your comedy The Clouds' (the reference was lost with Jowett's note); 'the general Laches'; 'heavy infantry'; 'making it obvious to anyone'; un-invert 'Many are the marvels' and 'those only are pursued who'; keep the pelican image and the escape.

evidence: "You may imagine Brasidas and others to have been like Achilles; or you may imagine Nestor and Antenor to have been like Pericles"
"they represent in a figure not only himself, but his words"
"smiths and cobblers and curriers"
"of the widest comprehension"
paragraphs.fix: Light: add a few identifying words (the Spartan general Brasidas; Nestor and Antenor, Homer's wise old counsellors; the statesman Pericles) so the pairings make sense; 'are an image of'; 'leather-workers' for 'curriers'; 'the widest scope'; keep the Silenus-bust image and 'the whole duty of a good and honorable man'.

evidence: "beginning as their lover he has ended by making them pay their addresses to him"
"Wherefore I say to you, Agathon"
"Be not deceived by him"
"do not be a fool and learn by experience, as the proverb says"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: make the role reversal explicit (he starts as their admirer and ends with them courting him); 'So'; 'Don't be deceived'; render the proverb so it warns against being the fool who learns only by getting hurt, not against learning from experience.

evidence: "or you would never have gone so far about to hide the purpose of your satyr's praises"
"only an ingenious circumlocution, of which the point comes in by the way at the end"
"you want to get up a quarrel between me and Agathon"
"the plot of this Satyric or Silenic drama has been detected"
"to set us at variance"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'gone to such roundabout lengths'; 'a clever roundabout story whose real point is slipped in at the end as if in passing'; 'stir up a quarrel'; a few words on satyr plays (the bawdy comic pieces staged after tragedies); 'turn us against each other'.

paragraphs.note: 'the couch below me' = the next place in the seating order; clear enough after 8.40.

evidence: "as you praised me, and I in turn ought to praise my neighbor on the right, he will be out of order in praising me again when he ought rather to be praised by me"
"I must entreat you to consent to this"
paragraphs.fix: Recast: spell out the seating rule in order (each speaker praises the man on his right; if Agathon lay between us he would have to praise me again, when it is my turn to praise him); 'I must ask you'.

paragraphs.note: 'Hurrah!' and 'that I may be praised' are dated but clear.

evidence: "no one else has any chance with the fair"
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'with the good-looking young men' ('the fair' can read as 'the fair sex' or 'fair-skinned'); keep 'specious reason'.

evidence: "The noise was tremendous"
"that they passed around from left to right"
"that the same person could be skilled at writing both comedy and tragedy"
paragraphs.fix: Light fidelity trim only: keep this modern rendering but delete two details not in Jowett ('The noise was tremendous', 'from left to right') and make 'could be skilled' state Jowett's claim that the gift for comedy is the same as for tragedy.
